Abstract
As a high-performance computing platform, the GPU is much suit-
able for cryptographic applications in cloud computing environ-
ment. Unfortunately, recent studies found that GPU-based AES
implementations are also vulnerable to cache-timing attacks. Al-
though those architectural-level and algorithmic-level countermea-
sures specifically tailored for power/electro-magnetic (EM) analysis
are effective to thwart the cache-timing attacks, they are either of
high cost or require customized hardware. In this work, we propose
a masking scheme, which is intrinsically device-independent, to
prevent GPU-based AES implementations from cache-timing at-
tacks with the full considerations of low cost and provable security.
The scheme reduces the requirement for random from linear to
constant number by taking the advantage of cache-timing leakage
model and, at the same time, maintains its security. The security
of the masking scheme is formally proved under realistic assump-
tions. In addition, we also present a typical GPU-based prototype
implementation of the scheme and evaluate the performance of
the implementation on CUDA-enabled GPUs of different architec-
tures. The results show that the performance of the implementation
varies from architecture to architecture. Nonetheless, all of them
outperform previous schemes.

Introduction
The demand for high-performance computing platform makes the
general-purpose Graphics Processing Unit (GPGPU) more popular
than ever. As a popular parallel computing device, the GPU is
well suited for accelerating security-sensitive applications in cloud
computing environment because of their highly efficient execution
paradigm named task-level parallelism (TLP). Unfortunately, recent
studies have found that GPU-based applications are susceptible
to many attacks [5, 6, 10–14]. Among those vulnerabilities cache-
timing attacks are the most serious ones, because they might be
conducted remotely [7, 8] in some situations. The cache-timing
attacks take advantage of the architectural drawbacks of the GPU
to completely recover the secret key of target implementations with
collected execution time of a program, so they are potentially great
threats to GPU-based cryptographic implementations.
A common countermeasure against timing attacks is designing
constant-time implementations, like the Montgomery ladder for
RSA or ECC. For GPU-based AES, this requires hardware changes
due to architectural timing variations. Another approach is adding
randomness to obscure the link between intermediate values and
execution time.
In 2018, Kadam et al. proposed a novel subwarp-based random-
ized coalescing technique to mitigate the timing channel vulnerabil-
ities [9]. In a sense, the approach takes both of the above ideas but
it is essentially a trade-off between security and performance, so a
complete protection of timing leakage with their method results
in remarkable performance degradation. Their countermeasure
is implemented on GPU-Sim [1], but what worse is it requires
architecturally-customized hardware, which makes their counter-
measure device-dependent in practice.
Since the architectural-level countermeasure is either high-cost
or not provably secure, we turn to masking countermeasures [2, 3],
which are widely used to counteract power/EM side-channel anal-
ysis, because of their device-independency and provable security.
The most intuitive way to apply a masking countermeasure to GPU-
based AES implementations is to take the threads as individuals
and apply a first-order masking scheme independently for each
thread. However, it may consumes too many random numbers and
requires too many masked tables, which is high-cost in both time
consumption and memory footprint.

In the light of this, we propose a novel masking countermea-
sure that is provably secure under realistic assumptions for typical
cache-timing attacks against GPU-based AES implementations. Our
contributions are three folds. Firstly, we propose a masking scheme
to prevent GPU-based AES implementations from cache-timing
attacks and prove the security of the scheme under realistic as-
sumptions. The scheme aims at low cost without compromising
the security. Particularly, for the first time we design a masked T-
table. Secondly, we propose a standard timer model and proves our
masking scheme under realistic assumptions. Thirdly, we realize
the masking scheme with a typical GPU-based prototype imple-
mentation and evaluate its performance on GPUs of three different
architectures.
2
Preliminary
2.1
CUDA-enabled GPU
CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is a parallel com-
puting platform and programming model developed by NVIDIA,
designed to harness the computational power of NVIDIA GPUs.
By providing an accessible programming model, CUDA allows de-
velopers to offload compute-intensive tasks to GPUs, significantly
accelerating performance compared to traditional CPU-based pro-
cessing. CUDA architecture is built around Streaming Multiproces-
sors (SMs), each containing multiple Scalar Processors (SPs), shared
memory, and a shared instruction unit. The key concept in CUDA
is the use of threads organized into warps (groups of 32 threads),
which execute instructions in a Single Instruction, Multiple Thread
(SIMT) manner. This enables efficient parallel execution across
thousands of threads in a GPU.
CUDA’s memory model includes various memory types, includ-
ing global memory, shared memory, constant memory, and registers,
all of which offer different trade-offs between latency and band-
width. Global memory is large but slow, while shared memory
provides faster access but is limited in size. CUDA supports a range
of memory optimizations, such as L1 and L2 caching, which can be
configured to improve memory access efficiency.

tract secret information like secret key by analyzing the measured
execution time. Until recently, timing attacks targeting GPU-based
cryptographic implementations were first studied [5, 7, 8]. Their
attacks can be performed remotely in some scenarios. Jiang et al.
proposed a timing attack based on the time leakage induced by
architectural drawbacks of GPUs called memory issue serialization
(MIS). MIS is described as follows for a constant number 푎.

Definition and Notations
Definition 1 For a side-channel attack to a multi-thread crypto-
graphic implementation, if an attacker can choose the number of
threads to run and provide the same random plaintexts to some

from} Chosen-Plaintext Side-Channel Attack (CPSCA).

3
Our Low-Cost Masking Scheme
Masking countermeasures are so promising that it is also applicable
to thwart cache-timing attacks against GPU-based AES implemen-
tations. However, an intuitive application of a masking scheme
always brings drawbacks. As the GPU features parallel execution
paradigm, the application of traditional masking scheme to a GPU-
based implementation involves the usage of multiple masks across
GPU threads. One direct approach is to take the threads as individu-
als and apply a first-order masking scheme independently for each
thread. Obviously, the approach can resist first-order EM/power
attacks against a GPU-based AES implementation, but it may not be
secure any more for cache-timing attacks and, at the same time, the
approach consumes too many random numbers and requires too
many masked tables, which is high-cost in both time consumption
and memory footprint.

3.1
A Masking Countermeasure
Now that the intuitive applications of traditional masking counter-
measures are of high cost, because the required numbers of random
are linear to the number of tasks. Hence, we aim at developing a
low-cost and provably secure masking countermeasure specific to
cache-timing attacks against GPU-based AES implementations.
The cost of a masking countermeasure for GPU-based AES im-
plementation consists of time consumption for random mask gen-
eration and memory footprint for masked LUT storage. In some
sense, a low consumption of random masks results in a low mem-
ory footprint, so a low-cost countermeasure cannot consume too
many masks. However, for the GPU, which always runs hundreds
of instances of encryption in parallel, it is really challengeable to
reduce the number of masks while not compromising the security.
We achieve the reduction of random numbers by mask reuse
among threads. The reuse of random masks among multiple threads
always reduces the security of a countermeasure, but our counter-
measure remains provably secure under realistic assumptions.
As the cache-timing leakage is induced by the collective TLU
operations within the execution, our masking scheme has to ran-
domize the indices of the TLU operations with the random bytes

3.2
Security Proof of the Masking Scheme
The security proof of masking countermeasures against EM analysis
is usually based on the probing model. The probing model assumes
that the side-channel leakage of any intermediate can be measured
by attackers, so an attacker is able to measure the leakages of
multiple intermediates if many EM probes are available. However,
unlike EM leakages, the execution time of a program is a one-
dimensional side-channel information. In other words, only a scalar
can be obtained as one time trace. Therefore, we coin a new term
called standard timer model (STM), which assumes only the total
execution time of a program can be obtained by attackers. Our
masking scheme will be proved under the STM.
To present a security proof of the masking countermeasure, we
give two assumptions, which are the basis of our proof.
Assumption 1: The time leakage of a GPU-based AES implemen-
tation is due to the memories shared among the threads within
thread warps. Each 32 (the size of a warp) of 푁threads access the
memories in a collective manner and therefore time leakage arises.

4
Prototype Implementation of Our Masking
Scheme
We consider efficient implementations using Γ-table on CUDA-
enabled GPUs. Besides time/memory cost and implementation
complexity, architectural features also impact performance. This
section presents a practical GPU-based prototype for our masking
scheme.
Random Numbers. Uniformly random numbers are essential
to masking countermeasures, which are generated on the host in
our implementations. Our masking scheme consumes very few
random bytes, precisely 160 bytes for a single GPU kernel emission.
For example, for the most popular NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU,
which has as many as 20 SMs of totally 2,560 cores, only 0.5 random
bit per thread are required on average if 2,560 tasks are started.
When the random bytes are ready on the host, they are copied into
a constant memory of GPUs.
Γ-table Implementation. Γ-table is the most important compo-
nent for our scheme. Since Γ-table is a non-linear transformation,
it has to be pre-computed off-line or computed on-line. When
the masked tables are implemented on the GPU, the location of
them does play a vital role to the overall performance. Generally
speaking, the tables can be stored into either the global memory or
shared memory of a GPU.
5
Performance Evaluation
For GPU tasks, the performance relies upon workloads and the
kernel configurations. We provide sufficient tasks with multiple
configurations. The throughout are showed in Table 1. The per-
formance loss of all the implementations on all the platforms are
much less than that in previous solution.
In addition, we analyze the memory footprint of our masking
scheme in Table 2. The global memory footprint of our counter-
measure is not important because GPUs are always equipped with
global memory of hundreds of megabytes. The shared memory
footprint of our countermeasure is the same as the unprotected
counterparts, which suggests that our countermeasure achieves
lower performance loss at no more memory costs.

Abstract: As a high-performance computing platform, the GPU is much suit- able for cryptographic applications in cloud computing environ- ment. Unfortunately, recent studies found that GPU-based AES implementations are also vulnerable to cache-timing attacks. Al- though those architectural-level and algorithmic-level countermea- sures specifically tailored for power/electro-magnetic (EM) analysis are effective to thwart the cache-timing attacks, they are either of high cost or require customized hardware. In this work, we propose a masking scheme, which is intrinsically device-independent, to prevent GPU-based AES implementations from cache-timing at- tacks with the full considerations of low cost and provable security. The scheme reduces the requirement for random from linear to constant number by taking the advantage of cache-timing leakage model and, at the same time, maintains its security. The security of the masking scheme is formally proved under realistic assump- tions. In addition, we also present a typical GPU-based prototype implementation of the scheme and evaluate the performance of the implementation on CUDA-enabled GPUs of different architec- tures. The results show that the performance of the implementation varies from architecture to architecture. Nonetheless, all of them outperform previous schemes.
